claims.text: Boole published The Mathematical Analysis of Logic in 1847, described as the first modern book on symbolic logic and little more than a pamphlet, containing his first efforts towards an algebraic logic of classes. It attracted very little attention outside his immediate circle, of which De Morgan was a member.

source.title: Boole, G., The Mathematical Analysis of Logic: Being an Essay Towards a Calculus of Deductive Reasoning, Macmillan, Barclay & Macmillan, Cambridge, 1847

claims.text: He expanded the idea in An Investigation of the Laws of Thought in 1854, whose core argument is that three operations — conjunction, disjunction and negation — suffice to perform all logical functions.

source.title: Boole, G., An Investigation of the Laws of Thought, Walton and Maberly, London, 1854

claims.text: For decades the ideas had no apparent practical application and were largely ignored. Shannon, working at MIT under Vannevar Bush on the electrical circuitry of a mechanical analogue computer, realised the algebra could be applied to circuit design, treating two-valued logical functions as switching gates.

source.title: Shannon, C. E., A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits, MIT master’s thesis 1937; Transactions of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers 57:713-723, 1938

claims.text: Shannon’s master’s thesis of 1937, A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits, applied the algebra to logic circuits built from electromechanical relays; he was twenty-one, and it was published in the Transactions of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers in 1938. It introduced switching algebra, allowing systematic design and optimisation of logical circuits.

source.title: Shannon, C. E., A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits, MIT master’s thesis 1937; Transactions of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers 57:713-723, 1938

beats.broke: two conditions can mean the same thing and look completely different, so you cannot tell whether a rewrite preserved behaviour by reading it
beats.fix: treat conditions as expressions in an algebra with laws, so equivalence becomes something you derive rather than something you judge
beats.cost: the algebraically simplest form is frequently the least readable, and says nothing about how the expression will be executed
beats.interview: what putting logic into algebra actually buys
